This seems rather wasteful to allocate new arrays over and over just to use as arguments.

Wouldn't `TextDecoder.decode` automatically make sure we use the fastest possible implementation?

Good call — switched to a module-level `TextDecoder('latin1')` singleton in 489ba74. Uses the engine's native implementation, eliminates both the chunk-loop allocations and the explicit subarray calls.

I went with `'latin1'` (Windows-1252 in WHATWG encoding spec) rather than the default UTF-8 to keep the mapping bijective — UTF-8 would produce replacement characters (U+FFFD) for byte sequences that aren't valid UTF-8, which could cause distinct binary values to compare equal. Windows-1252 maps every byte value 0–255 to a unique code point, so the comparable-string guarantee holds for taint tracking.

for very long arrays this will do quite a bit of memory work and much of it potentially repeated since the entire tail is continued into each new task. If we're already making affordances for this notion we might as well support rendering from an index to avoid memory churn

Have just pushed up [a commit that does this approach](https://github.com/facebook/react/pull/36053/commits/071f0c7ac72ef4dbe1c0ba9e3b31130c13edff8c)

I didn't change the `createTask` signature for the extra properties (as this is the only place they're used), but I can do it that way if prefered.

Also let me know if you'd prefer a separate branch / PR for this instead

Sorry for the delay, I’ve been unwell. I replaced the spread operator with explicit object construction to avoid extra copies. Let me know if this solves the issue for you.
I don't think this check is an optimization tbh. it's checked in `parseModelString` and will just return the value there.

The check is duplicated, but the point is avoiding the function call. `parseModelString` is a large function with many switch cases, so neither GCC nor V8 will inline it. Without the guard, every non-`$` string (class names, text content, attribute values, etc.) pays for argument setup, stack frame push/pop, the same `value[0] === '$'` check inside, and return. With the guard, those strings never enter the function. I haven't measured the impact though, so it would be good to verify with your benchmarks.

Curious about the performance comparison here vs. the initial version's element shortcut. The shortcut avoided the generic loop for element arrays entirely, processing type/key/props with type-specific knowledge (e.g. skipping `_walkJSON` for a plain string type or null key), avoiding `'' + i` string conversion per index, and not re-reading fields from the array through `parseModelTuple`. With the post-loop approach, element arrays go through the full generic walk, then `parseModelTuple` re-accesses all fields that were just walked. Was there a measured reason to drop the shortcut, or was it just for simplicity?

> Was there a measured reason to drop the shortcut, or was it just for simplicity?

Yeah the reason is the existing tests fail if the loop is moved afterwards 😄

The reason is that `value[0]` is a string, not the `REACT_ELEMENT_TYPE` symbol.

I checked and in the various benchmarks this change did not make things meaningfully slower while it preserves the existing behavior / check which is why moving it made sense for this PR.

I think we can change the check the string instead and this fast path can be unlocked, but I'm not familiar enough with this code to properly asses that it would be safe to make that assumption. Hence matching the existing behavior that passes the tests.

There can be performance benefits to having these be inline because when the type / hidden class check is done in the VM it can share that check with other code around the same place instead of having to check it again for the next member access inside that branch.


It's not always better depending on how unusual the code path is, but that's why I favor always having these inline in most cases.
We shouldn't create the closure outside the condition. Maybe it's optimized but we should make sure.
But it's used in both branches of the condition.
In that case you should move it out to a reusable function in module scope and then call that from the closure. So that the closure only needs to be allocated in the delayed branch.
Then `addDebugInfo` can be hoisted out.

try/catch is notorious for deopting. It's better in modern browsers but can still trigger extra stuff on the stack and avoid inlining capabilities by making larger code.

We need to cut everything. We should just let it throw if this is not supported.

I'm concerned about this unnecessary condition adding to code size (in terms of memory / JIT optimization and not download size) and the extra lookup every call.

We should make two entire copies of the function and switch which function we use instead so that the function that we use doesn't have to make any additional checks at runtime.

Alternatively we should just assume that you can set it and not support environments that don't play ball.
